tagline: Time tracking with screenshots, activity scores and payroll attached.
verdictSummary: What Hubstaff sells is not a timer, it is a chain that ends in money moving: tracked hours, an activity score, an approved timesheet, and an automatic payment to a contractor in another country. The paying half needs money-transmission partners and the monitoring half needs software installed on machines you administer and a lawful basis to watch people work. Neither belongs in a personal build. The consolation build here monitors exactly one person: you.
coreLoopDIY: Measure your own working patterns locally — active application, idle detection, and a focus score — with everything staying on your machine and nobody else able to see it.
whatYouLose: tracking anyone but yourself, which is the entire commercial product
automatic payments to contractors through payroll partners
timesheet approval workflows and locked pay periods
the mobile and desktop apps published and signed by a vendor
whyPeopleStillPay: Because paying twelve contractors in nine countries from approved timesheets is a compliance and payments problem, not a tracking problem, and Hubstaff has the partners for it.
prompt:
Build a personal activity monitor. It watches one machine — yours — and nothing leaves it.

Be explicit in the README about scope: this is self-measurement. Deploying anything like it on other people's machines raises consent and employment-law obligations that differ by country and are not a technical matter.

Stack: a small desktop agent plus a local web dashboard. Any language with OS-level window APIs; SQLite for storage; everything on localhost with no remote endpoint at all.

The agent samples every few seconds and records: the active application, the window title, and whether input has occurred since the last sample. It never captures screen content and never records keystrokes — say so in the README and mean it.

Derived measures:
- **Idle**: no input for longer than a configurable threshold ends the current block. On return, prompt once for what that gap was, with options to discard it, mark it as a break, or assign it to a project.
- **Sessions**: contiguous activity in one category, with a minimum length so a two-second glance at a browser does not fragment an hour of work.
- **Context switches per hour**, which is a more honest attention measure than any single focus score.
- **Categories**: you assign applications and window-title patterns to categories yourself. Ship no default classification — an inherited productivity rating is somebody else's opinion about your work.

Privacy controls, first-class rather than an afterthought:
- A pause button that stops sampling entirely, with the paused periods visible as such rather than silently missing.
- Per-application title redaction: for chosen apps, store only the application name, never the window title.
- Retention: raw samples are deleted after N days by default, leaving only the aggregates. Make N small.
- One command that deletes everything.

Dashboard: a day timeline, category totals, context switches per hour, and a week-over-week trend. CSV export.

Write tests for idle detection at the threshold boundary, for session merging with a short interruption, and for retention actually removing raw rows.

Do not add remote reporting, screenshots, keystroke logging, or any way to observe another machine.

faq.q: Why refuse screenshots when the paid product has them?
faq.a: Because a local screenshot archive is a liability with no upside for self-measurement — it captures passwords, private messages and client data — and because the moment you build it, the tool becomes something you could point at someone else.

faq.q: Why ship no default app classification?
faq.a: Because "productive" is contextual: a browser is research for one person and procrastination for another, and inheriting a vendor's ratings is how these tools produce numbers that feel unfair. Ten minutes of self-classification is more accurate than any default.

faq.q: Is monitoring employees legal if I build it myself?
faq.a: It depends heavily on jurisdiction, and building it yourself removes none of the obligations. In much of Europe, continuous monitoring needs a documented lawful basis, proportionality, and notice to the people monitored. That is why this prompt is scoped to your own machine.

faq.q: What does the two-seat minimum mean in practice?
faq.a: That the advertised $4.99 is never the real floor — the cheapest Hubstaff account is two seats, so about $9.98 a month on annual billing, even for a solo user.
